html:
East Prussia was the easternmost province of Prussia and of Germany, on the Baltic coast around Königsberg, now Kaliningrad. It is shown here in 1920 and 1930, when it was cut off from the rest of Germany.

The land had been conquered from the Baltic Prussians by the Teutonic Knights in the 13th century. It became the Duchy of Prussia in 1525, and its dukes in Berlin later made it the core of the Prussian kingdom. Immanuel Kant spent his whole life in Königsberg. In 1914 the Germans stopped a Russian invasion here at the Battle of Tannenberg.

After the First World War the Treaty of Versailles gave Poland a corridor to the sea, so East Prussia became an exclave. The Memel district was taken away. In 1920 plebiscites in its southern districts voted to stay German. In 1945 the Red Army overran it, and most Germans fled or were driven out in the expulsion of Germans. Its south went to Poland and its north to the Soviet Union.
